items.title: Unpacking the AI hype: brave new world?
items.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a buzzword for decades, yet we find ourselves in a new wave of AI hype, one that holds a genuine promise to reshape how we live and work. What sets this era apart? While it might seem like nothing much has changed, there’s both a technical evolution and a shift in accessibility that are driving the current shift. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a buzzword for decades, yet we find ourselves in a new wave of AI hype, one that holds a genuine promise to reshape how we live and work. What sets this era apart? While it might seem like nothing much has changed, there’s both a technical evolution and a shift in accessibility that are driving the current shift. Jasper Masemann, investment partner at Cherry Ventures, and Lutz Finger, venture partner at Cherry Ventures discuss exactly why is this new AI hype so special in our latest podcast episode. Technologically, the foundation of AI—sequence prediction in natural language processing—has been around for a while. Consider this: if we talk about Forrest Gump and say, "Life is like a box of...," most people will predict "chocolates." But this prediction hinges on context. Early models struggled with maintaining context over long sentences. The advent of attention models has transformed this by allowing AI to focus on the most relevant parts of lengthy inputs, improving accuracy in tasks like language translation and text generation. So, the core concept hasn’t changed; it’s the implementation that has seen significant refinement. The most profound shift, however, is in usability. AI, particularly through tools like ChatGPT, has become accessible to everyone. Previously, leveraging AI required specialized knowledge and resources. You'd need a data scientist from a top institution to set up models and process data. Today, anyone can input a query into ChatGPT and receive a coherent response in seconds. AI is no longer just a tool for experts; it’s a utility for the masses, which explains the surge in its adoption and the accompanying hype. The democratization of AI technology is a game-changer. But it's crucial to temper this enthusiasm with an understanding of AI’s limitations. AI models, while impressive, operate on historical data and probabilistic predictions. They excel at generating human-like text but fall short in understanding context as humans do. For instance, an AI might predict Lutz’s preference for Costa Rican coffee based on his past behavior, but it can’t grasp the nuance of changing tastes or the emotional experiences associated with coffee. Moreover, AI's way of learning is fundamentally different from learning in humans. Humans develop a gut feeling from experiences and can explain their reasoning—a car changing lanes haphazardly is interpreted as a danger sign based on past observations. AI, on the other hand, makes decisions based on statistical likelihoods without true comprehension. In conclusion, while the core principles of AI remain unchanged, enhancements in technology and significant improvements in accessibility have sparked the current hype. As we embrace this powerful technology, it’s essential to recognize its limitations and continue refining its capabilities. AI’s journey is far from over, and its potential is vast, but so are its challenges. Tune in to The Edge , our very own podcast breaking down the latest AI developments, to explore these insights and more! At Cherry, she’ll work side-by-side our founders helping them in matters involving recruiting global top talent, hyper growth, and scaling. Let’s meet Louisa 👇 Joining Cherry represents your first move into venture capital. What are you most looking forward to in working at Cherry and with our portfolio? I’m very excited about a role where I can now devote my time helping founders unleash their potential in building exceptional companies. I’ve had the luxury of working with executive leadership for most of my career, I’ve built up 1–2 man startups to support companies through hyper growth, and there have been so many learnings along the way. No matter what stage you are at, there are challenges at all levels of hiring. There are also different challenges and milestones a founder will encounter at different stages of growth. So, being able to hold companies’ hands through these changes and considerations is very rewarding. What do you enjoy most in working in the talent sphere? It’s one of those careers that is always evolving and there are new approaches, new products, and ways of working. You’ve hit the nail on the head as to why I enjoy it so much. It’s one of those career paths where you are continually learning as the industry evolves. Aside from uncovering the best talent, another passion is building a culture where people can be their best selves. Organizational design and its impact on performance fascinates me. I’ve seen a lot of approaches and the different degrees of impact on employees, good and bad. We invest in young companies. What are the 2–3 most important hiring considerations founders need to consider regarding talent early on? Have an eye on building diversity in your top levels early on . Your first hires are your talent magnets for future hires. Get it right early — and you’ll have an amazing competitive advantage. Hire for resilience and a growth mindset . Think about what you need the role in your company to achieve. What does success look like in the next 6–12 months? Don’t be bamboozled by education (a diversity killer) or a great sounding company name (what made them successful there, may not make them successful with you). Explore the problem you want to solve and hire the best person that can help you solve it. Make finding and introducing great talent to your company a KPI for all your employees. Put it in the job description, your performance reviews, let it become part of your DNA. Don’t make any one team responsible for the growth of your company — it should be everyone’s responsibility to build a great team. How has tech hiring changed over your career? When I started in 1996, I worked in the City of London and my clients were investment banks. I didn’t have a computer. Candidate files were stored in a metal filing cabinet. I would mostly walk candidate profiles over to my clients, fax, or post them. Candidates were sourced via headhunting — literally calling up hundreds of banks, getting through reception (in a very creative ways) and navigating your way through the company to find the person you needed. You would research physical business magazines, yellow pages (business phone directory), place adverts in newspapers and most importantly references through your network. Within a year the first computer arrived on my desk and I was immediately hooked. Google did not even exist at this stage. I used a searching tool called Hoover where I was able to uncover even more information on companies (but only if they too had a presence). Then there was the invention of job boards, which was interesting to watch. A lot of people thought it would be the end of the recruitment industry but instead it just blossomed. For me, however, it’s always been about building strong communities and research. So I quickly jumped on the social network sites before Facebook even existed. For me, these were great connection tools. And then around 1999–2000 there was this tiny beta platform I came across called LinkedIn. It wasn’t what we know today. It was a peer-to-peer exchange of business contacts — I was hooked! I think today it’s slightly tarnished by lazy recruiting tactics, such as spamming people with inappropriate roles, where the recruiter clearly has not even looked at their profile they are contacting. However, it still holds a lot of value if used correctly, in conjunction with other tools of course. You are missing a trick if you only use this tool for headhunting. I’ve also always tried to seek out new tools that give me the competitive edge, away from where regular people would look. The internet is a researcher’s dream. I saw the rise of GitHub repositories — another amazing tool for connecting with tech talent. There are now tools to create nurture campaigns and I love where the business is going around automation and increasing productivity. Will all this ever replace humans? items.text: 2021 is off to a great start at Cherry Ventures with the addition of Maximilian Brückner to the investment team. Max embraces all things Founders First and will no doubt be an asset to our portfolio, bringin... Max joins our Berlin base and will work across deals, but is particularly interested in regulated industries, improving the legal software stack, and cybersecurity. He will also support our Nordic coverage. Max recently completed an internship with us at Cherry and we were immediately impressed. He showed drive, speed, and analytical rigor in deals plus a commitment to founders and a positive “can do” attitude. Long story short, we jumped at the opportunity to bring him on board full-time. Max studied law at Humboldt University in Berlin and the University of Barcelona and gained previous work experience at Acton Capital, Freshfields, and Zenjob. items.title: Welcoming our new investment hires and venture partners
items.text: As we’ve said before, founders first is more than a motto. It’s a mindset that we look for in current and prospective team members and... As we’ve said before, founders first is more than a motto. It’s a mindset that we look for in current and prospective team members and partnerships. With that, we’d like to introduce new investors and venture partners who embody this approach and are joining Cherry Ventures. Together, they bring a wealth of experience in angel and early-stage investing, deep operator roots, entrepreneurial know-how, and deep rooted passion for diversity and inclusion in tech. These attributes — plus many others too countless to list — will be a powerful part of our growing team, investments and portfolio, and presence in Europe. Well, without any further ado, let’s meet them: Based in London, Dinika Mahtani joins us as a Principal. She previously spent four years at Uber working across multiple business lines, most recently as General Manager of JUMP UK (e-bikes and scooters) and the founding team of UberEats EMEA. Immediately prior to Cherry, Dinika spent a year in the climate tech space at Kaluza, part of the Ovo Group (inc. Vertical Aerospace), a SaaS platform focused on electric grid optimization. Dinika spent her formative years in the US, where she started her career in investment banking. Along the way, she’s become an active angel investor in and advisor to female-founded startups. “Early-stage venture is a people business, and Cherry is people first,” says Dinika. “I’m beyond excited to build upon the existing VC ecosystem in the UK, supporting founders across all backgrounds.” A neuroscientist by training, Nicole Lai is also joining our investment team based in London. She most recently worked at European investment firm Atomico. There, she focused on Series A deep tech and enterprise investments. Before moving to Europe, Nicole worked as an investor at Real Ventures, an early-stage VC in Canada, where she also calls home. She started her career as the Scientific Project Lead at Moonshot Health, a developer of scientifically validated digital biomarkers. At Cherry, Nicole brings longstanding interests in health, sustainability, computational biology, and privacy-preserving technologies. “Having made the transition from academia and tech transfer to startup to early-stage VC and then Series A VC, I wanted to come back and focus on pre-seed and seed,” says Nicole. “Working with founders at an earlier stage is where I can combine my experiences and have the most impact.” Marie Outtier and Josefin Landgård are joining Cherry Ventures as venture partners and will focus on supporting our French, UK, and Nordic coverage in terms of geographies plus much more. They’ll also support our companies with their entrepreneurial know-how in the scaling of their companies. Marie co-founded and led Aiden.ai as CEO. The AI-powered marketing analyst that helps growth marketers at SMBs by generating optimization recommendations across Facebook, Snap, Google Ads and Twitter. The startup was acquired by Twitter in 2019, where she is now director of product management. Marie is also an angel investor in 20 startups across Europe and the US, 40% of which have diverse founders. “The European startup ecosystem needs to see more operators become investors. Having met with over 100 founders in the last 18 months, we have no shortage of talent and ambition in Europe,” says Marie. “We now have large volumes of capital available too, but what we need is experience from the trenches getting shared with early-stage startups. This is what I see when I look at the Cherry team.” Josefin co-founded and led KRY as CEO and COO. Kry is a European leader in digital healthcare, providing patients with the means to see a doctor via video or chat on their smartphone or tablet. Now, Josefin is CEO of MANTLE, a CBD-focused wellbeing company she founded in 2019. In the new year, we’ll have more exciting team updates to share. But we’re immensely excited to be joined by these four women as we at Cherry and our portfolio continues to grow and play a part in Europe’s thriving ecosystem.
